How much to charge for dryer vent cleaning

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$99 dryer vent special.” That number is not a takeoff. A one-story wall cap with eight feet of pipe is not the same job as a two-story roof cap with a 28-foot run and a camera pass. The word “dryer vent” is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the stories and the run, not just the special

HVAC-maintenance calculators price filter, coil, and a seasonal visit. Chimney-sweep calculators price flue, creosote, and a CSIA sweep. Kitchen-hood calculators price a restaurant canopy and a rooftop fan. Appliance-repair calculators price the machine. A dryer-vent job is a lint takeoff: the included wall cap, the extra story the coupon never mentions, the extra feet of duct, and the roof cap. Quoting all of that from a published special is how the first extra story eats the field margin.

A job with a similar first dryer can cost much more

Each extra story is a taller ladder, a second-floor access, and time that never appears on the coupon. Extra feet over the included eight-foot run are billed as their own hours and extra rods. A rooftop termination, a camera pass, crushed flex in the laundry closet, a nest, and occupied-home access are adders that get forgotten on a wall-cap special. On the sample rates a 2-story roof cap with a 28 ft run, a camera pass, and occupied access prices about $545 ($19.45 per foot, 3.5 crew-hours). The same shop’s 8 ft one-story wall cap prices about $178 ($22.29 per foot, 1.2 hours, walk-away $128). Matching a $99 Facebook special on the roof job is how that job becomes a loss of about $293.

A duplex laundry is not automatically the expensive one

A 2-story duplex laundry with two extra dryers, 22 ft of run, a camera pass, crushed-flex replacement, a nest, and occupied access is not the roof cap plus 20%. On the sample rates that multi-dryer job prices about $704 ($235 per dryer, 5.4 crew-hours) — more as a total, less per dryer, because the extra dryers and the nest do not live in a published multi-unit adder. A typical 2-story wall/soffit with an 18 ft run prices about $273 (2.2 hours). Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first extra story.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $38/h tech loaded at 32% payroll burden is $50.16. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. On the sample rates even the brochure wall cap walk-away is $128, which is why a $99 coupon is already a loss of about $29 before the first extra story. Replace every rate with your brush and rod invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a fire inspection, a building-code determination, a lint-clearance certificate, a guarantee that any dryer will not overheat, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. Job type, stories, run length, dryer count, and whether the house needs a rooftop termination are yours to confirm.

Price your next job

Common questions

How much to charge for dryer vent cleaning?

Charge from the included one-story wall cap, extra stories over that include, extra feet of duct over the included short run, extra dryers, a rooftop termination, camera inspection, crushed-flex replacement, nest or blockage, occupied-home access, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 1-story wall cap at the sample rates in this calculator prices around $178 — about $178 per dryer.

Why is a flat $99 dryer-vent special dangerous?

Homeowners count 'a dryer vent is a dryer vent.' Extra stories, extra feet, extra dryers, a roof cap, a camera pass, crushed flex, and a nest do not live in a $99 coupon. Matching a cheaper wall-cap quote written for a brochure ranch is how a roof job becomes a loss.

Does a longer run always cost more to clean?

Not in proportion. On the sample rates a 2-story roof cap with a 28 ft run, a camera pass, and occupied access prices around $545 ($19.45 per foot), while an 8 ft one-story wall cap prices around $178 ($22.29 per foot).

No warranty. This page and the calculator are free and as-is. They are not fire-safety, building-code, construction, appliance, legal, tax, or financial advice. You are responsible for verifying every figure before you rely on it or send a bid.

Where the hours go

    Where the cost goes

      Hand the customer a proposal

      The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

      Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

      Common questions

      What does this dryer vent estimate include?

      The price adds up loaded labor for the base setup plus every extra story and extra foot of run beyond the ones you mark as included, extra dryers, a camera pass, crushed-flex replacement, a nest or heavy blockage, occupied-home access, and site/travel time — plus the brush kit, rod material, camera fee, flex kit, nest disposal, and a roof safety kit on roof-cap jobs, then overhead and your target margin. Nothing is a flat “$99 special” regardless of scope.

      Why do stories and run feet only bill past what's “included”?

      Every job type already assumes a base setup — the one-story wall cap the presets call the $99 special — so “stories included” and “run feet included” are the first story and first few feet that base setup already covers. Only stories and feet beyond those thresholds add hours, which is why a two-story roof-cap job with a 28-foot run prices well above the one-story special even though both start from the same base setup hours.

      Why does the job type change the base setup hours but not the per-story or per-foot rate?

      Job type (wall-cap, two-story, roof-cap, or multi-dryer) only re-suggests the base setup hours — a roof termination simply takes longer to safely access than a wall cap before any story or footage is even counted. Extra-story, extra-foot, extra-dryer, camera, flex, nest, and occupied hours are separate line items you set once and reuse across every job type.

      What do camera, flex replacement, nest, and occupied-home add beyond labor hours?

      Each is both an hours line and, where it applies, a materials line: camera adds inspection hours plus a camera fee, flex replacement adds hours plus a flex-kit cost, and a nest or blockage adds removal hours plus a disposal cost. Occupied-home only adds hours (extra care and cleanup around a resident), with no separate material cost.

      Is my data uploaded anywhere?

      No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. A share link encodes only the inputs you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us; only your business name and contact details for the printed proposal are kept in this browser's local storage, and “Forget my business details” clears them.

      Does this check fire safety, code compliance, or whether a dryer is safe to run?

      No. Hours and kit costs are ballpark shop figures you can edit, not a fire inspection, a building-code determination, a lint-clearance certificate, or a guarantee that any dryer will not overheat. Cleaning restores airflow through the existing duct; whether the routing or material itself meets current code is a separate judgment call for the site visit.

vs-a-flat-99-dollar-special.html.text:
← Dryer Vent Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $99 dryer vent special

A "$99 dryer vent special" is not a price for a dryer vent clean — it is a coupon-page number, and on this calculator's own arithmetic it doesn't even clear the one-story wall cap it's named for.

What a flat $99 special is

A flat dollar figure is the fastest thing to put on a flyer or a coupon site: one number, easy to remember, and the number a caller holding a competitor's ad will ask you to match on their own house.

The number behind it was set to sound cheap, not to cover the shortest job it could describe — and then quoted again for every house afterward, whether or not the next one has a second story, a longer duct run, an extra dryer, a camera pass, crushed flex to replace, a nest to clear, or a roof cap to access.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the job type, stories, duct run, extra dryers, a camera pass, flex replacement, a nest or blockage, occupied-home access, and your own wage, material, and overhead rates. It prices the base setup, every story and foot beyond it, extra dryers, and each extra separately, and returns a break-even price and price per dryer below which the job loses money — for this house, not a flyer number.

Job$99 specialBreak-even priceVerdict
1-story wall cap, 8 ft run, 1 dryer (the flat special's own job)$99.00$128.39Short $29.39
2-story wall or soffit, 18 ft run, 1 dryer$99.00$196.45Short $97.45
Roof cap, 2 stories, 28 ft run, camera pass, occupied home$99.00$392.14Short $293.14
Duplex laundry, 2 extra dryers, 22 ft run, camera, flex, nest, occupied$99.00$507.23Short $408.23

Worked using this calculator's own shipped defaults: a $38 hourly wage, 32% payroll burden, 16% overhead on direct cost, and the job type's own suggested base-setup hours — not numbers invented for this page. Open the calculator to check any row yourself.

Notice the first row: it is the exact job the flat rate is named for — the shortest wall-cap run this calculator can describe — and it is already $29.39 short of break-even before a second story, an extra foot of duct, or a single extra is added. Every row after that only widens the gap.

What a flat $99 special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same figure whether the job is a one-story wall cap with eight feet of pipe or a two-story roof cap with a 28-foot run and a camera pass. Prices a base setup, then adds hours for every story and foot of run beyond it, so a longer, higher job costs more than a short one.
Has no separate line for a second or third dryer sharing the same laundry closet. Adds hours per extra dryer beyond the first, and reports the price per dryer alongside the total.
Prices "a dryer vent" the same whether or not a camera pass, crushed-flex replacement, or a nest is involved. Adds hours and a materials fee for a camera pass, flex replacement, and a nest or blockage only when each applies.
Has no line for a roof-cap termination's safety kit or the extra care an occupied home needs. Adds a roof safety kit on roof-cap jobs and extra hours for occupied-home access when either applies.
Gives the homeowner a number to shop, not a figure to check a quote against when their house turns out to be two stories with a nest in the vent after the flat rate was already promised. Reports the break-even price and price per dryer for the job as entered, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before it is confirmed.

A flat $99 special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is quoted for a job it was never priced on, and "a dryer vent" alone never tells you that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why doesn't a flat $99 dryer vent special cover its own job?

Because the $99 figure is usually set to sound cheap on a flyer, not derived from loaded labor, brush and rod material, and overhead for the exact one-story wall-cap job it is named for. On this calculator's own defaults — a $38 hourly wage, 32% burden, 16% overhead, and the job's own base-setup and travel hours — the simplest possible job it could describe, a one-story wall cap with an eight-foot run and one dryer, already breaks even at $128.39: $29.39 more than the flat rate before a single extra story, foot, or dryer is added.

What does a flat $99 special usually leave out entirely?

Every story and foot of run beyond the shortest possible setup, extra dryers, a camera pass, crushed-flex replacement in the laundry closet, a bird nest or heavy blockage, occupied-home access, and a roof-cap termination's safety kit. A published flat number is set on one configuration — usually the shortest wall-cap run a coupon page can advertise — and has no separate line for any of those.

How much do extra stories, run feet, and extras actually add over a flat special?

On this calculator's own worked examples, at a $38 hourly wage, 32% burden, 16% overhead, and the form's own shipped rates: a two-story wall or soffit job with an 18-foot run and one dryer breaks even at $196.45, $97.45 short of a $99 special. A roof-cap termination with two stories, a 28-foot run, a camera pass, and occupied-home access breaks even at $392.14, $293.14 short. A duplex laundry with two extra dryers, a camera pass, flex replacement, a nest, and occupied access breaks even at $507.23, $408.23 short.

Is a flat $99 special ever the right way to price a dryer vent job?

On this calculator's own numbers, not even the shortest job it can describe clears it: a one-story wall cap with an eight-foot run and one dryer already breaks even $29.39 above the flat rate. The gap only widens from there as stories, run feet, extra dryers, a camera pass, flex replacement, a nest, or occupied-home access are added, because a flat per-job number has no way to see any of them until the tech is already on the ladder.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local labor rates or what competitors charge. It takes the job type, stories, run feet, extra dryers, camera pass, flex replacement, nest, occupied access, and your own wage, burden, and overhead, and turns them into a break-even price for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat special skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat $99 special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the shortest run it was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

This calculator vs. WePro

Two different shapes: WePro is a subscription field-service app for running a dryer-vent cleaning company's scheduling, dispatch, and invoicing. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one job cost, given its stories, run length, and extras, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

WePro is a field-service app built for dryer vent and duct cleaning companies. It schedules cleanings, dispatches the right tech with job details and notes, tracks work in progress with real-time status updates from the field, sends customers appointment reminders and on-the-way messages, and turns completed jobs into invoices and customer-ready service reports. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. WePro's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — a field-service platform for dryer-vent and duct cleaning companies, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for WePro appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what WePro does. It does not schedule techs, dispatch jobs, or send customer messages, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes the job type — 1-story wall cap, 2-story wall or soffit, roof-cap termination, or a multi-dryer duplex laundry — the stories and run feet beyond a base setup, extra dryers, a camera pass, crushed-flex replacement, a nest or blockage, occupied-home access, loaded wage, brush kit and rod material, camera and flex kit fees, nest disposal, a roof safety kit on roof jobs, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the price, the price per dryer, the price per foot, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a copyable customer-facing bid summary.
